Introduction: Light and Distance
For as long as ships have sailed close to land, sailors have needed to
know where the land ends. A coastline that is obvious by day disap
pears at night, and a harbour entrance that is easy to find in calm
weather becomes a trap in a storm. The earliest answer was simple:
a fire on a hill
, kept burning by whoever lived nearest.
This essay asks two plain questions: how did a fire on a hill become
a tower with a lens, and why did it take so long? The short answer
is that a light is only useful if it can be seen far away and recognised
for what it is. Both problems turned out to be harder than building
the tower. The lens is discussed in
the section on the lens
I. Fires and towers
The first towers were little more than raised fireplaces. Wood and
coal burned unevenly, smoke hid the flame, and a keeper had to climb
the stairs every few hours to feed the fire. On a clear night such a
light could be seen for a few miles; in rain, hardly at all.
Oil lamps were cleaner but weaker. Keepers tried polished metal
behind the flame to throw the light forward, and for a while every
new tower used a slightly larger mirror than the last. The improve

A light that cannot be told apart from the others is almost worse
than no light.

II. The lens
The real change came with the stepped lens: rings of glass arranged
so that almost all of the lamp’s light leaves the tower as one narrow
beam. A small flame behind a good lens could now be seen further
than a large fire on an open hill.
The first effect was range: lights could be placed further from
danger and still be useful.
The second was identity: each tower got its own pattern of flashes,
printed on the charts.
The third was cost: lenses were expensive, so fewer, better towers
replaced many small ones.

III. Keepers and machines
For a long time every light needed a keeper. The work was regular and
lonely: trimming wicks, winding the clockwork that turned the lens,
cleaning soot from the glass every morning.

What has not changed is the purpose. A lighthouse still says the same
three things it always said: here is the land, here is the danger, and

Conclusion
The history of the lighthouse is mostly a history of seeing further
with less: less fuel, less labour, less guesswork for the people at sea.
